passages.t: Walk worthy: ‘one body and one Spirit’
passages.happening:
Here the letter turns. For three chapters Paul has praised God for what he has done. Now he says what that means for daily life.

“As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (verse 1). That walk begins with how believers treat one another: “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (verse 2), working hard “to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace” (verse 3).

Then Paul gives the reason, in a list of seven ‘ones’: “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all” (verses 4-6).
passages.hearers:
The little word ‘then’ in verse 1 matters. It ties everything in chapters 4 to 6 to everything in chapters 1 to 3. Believers do not walk worthy in order to be called. They walk worthy because they already have been called, chosen, forgiven and made one people.

Notice that the first thing Paul asks for is not a great deed. It is humility, gentleness and patience, the quiet habits that let people who are very different live together. They are the habits of Jesus himself, who calls himself ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (Matthew 11:29).

Also notice what Paul says about unity. He does not tell them to make it. He tells them to ‘preserve’ it, to guard something the Spirit has already made. A church does not create its oneness by agreeing on everything. It receives oneness from God and then works hard not to break it.

The seven ‘ones’ are built around the Spirit, the Lord Jesus and the Father. Many readers think Paul is using words the churches already said together, a kind of early confession. Either way, the shape is the same one the church would later confess in its creeds: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The church's unity rests on the unity of God.
passages.ot:
The first words of Israel's daily confession were about God being one: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Paul's ‘one Lord’ and ‘one God and Father of all’ stand on that confession, now spoken with the Son and the Spirit in view.

The Psalms sing the goodness of a people at peace with one another: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1).

And the prophets looked for a day when many peoples would come to the God of Jacob together: “He will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths” (Isaiah 2:3). Paul's ‘walk’ is that old picture of a life lived on God's road.
passages.asks: Paul asks for humility, gentleness and patience before he asks for anything else. Ask which of the three comes hardest to you, and with whom. Ask whether you have treated the unity of your church as something to guard, or as something that only holds when others agree with you. And ask who in your church you need to bear with in love this week.

passages.happening:
Paul moves from what all believers share to what each one is given. “Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ” (verse 7).

He backs this up with a psalm: “This is why it says: ‘When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men’” (verse 8).

Then he comments on one word of it. “What does ‘He ascended’ mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth?” (verse 9). “He who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Every reader in the Roman world knew the picture behind verse 8. A victorious king or general came home in a parade, with prisoners of war led behind him, and he shared out the treasure he had won.

Paul uses that picture for Jesus. The one who went up is the risen Christ, who has won the victory over the powers of evil (1:20-22). He leads captives in his train, the enemies he has beaten. And he does what a winning king does: he gives gifts to his people.

The word ‘grace’ in verse 7 is used here in a special way. It means the particular gift, or calling, that Christ gives to each believer. No one is left out (‘each one of us’), and no one is given everything. The gifts are measured out by Christ, not earned.

Verse 10 says why he went up: ‘in order to fill all things’. Christ's going up was not going away. It was taking his place as Lord over the whole creation, so that his presence and rule reach everywhere.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Psalm 68, a song of God marching in victory from Sinai to his holy place: “the Lord is in His sanctuary as He was at Sinai” (Psalm 68:17). The next verse says, “You have ascended on high; You have led captives away. You have received gifts from men” (Psalm 68:18).

Notice the difference. In the psalm the victor receives gifts. In Ephesians he gives them. Paul is not careless here. An old Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms, known from copies made centuries later, also has ‘gave’, so Paul may be following a way the verse was already read. And a king who receives tribute in victory then shares it with his people, so the two pictures belong together. Paul reads the psalm in the light of Christ: the God who went up in victory has now come in his Son, and the Son shares his spoils with his people.
passages.hard:
‘He also descended to the lower parts of the earth’ (verse 9). Where did he go down to? Christians have read this in more than one way, and these notes do not choose.

Many readers take it to mean his coming down from heaven to earth when he was born as a man. On this reading ‘the lower parts of the earth’ means ‘the lower parts, that is, the earth’, the world below heaven. The point is that the one who went up is the same one who first came down to us. That fits verse 10, and John's words about “the One who descended from heaven” (John 3:13).

Other readers take it to mean his going down into death: to the grave, or to the realm of the dead, between his death and his rising. They point out that the Psalms speak of ‘the depths of the earth’ as the place where the dead go (Psalm 63:9). Some link it with 1 Peter 3:19 and with the line in the Apostles' Creed, ‘he descended into hell’, whose older sense, as the site's note on the creed says, is that he descended to the dead. That line, at least, guards the plain truth that Jesus really died.

A few readers think of Christ coming down again at Pentecost in the gift of the Spirit, since the gifts follow next.

What all of these readings agree on is the heart of the passage. The one who reigns over all is the one who first came all the way down for us. There is no depth of the earth, or of death, that he did not go to, and no height to which he has not been raised.
passages.asks: Paul says that grace has been given to ‘each one of us’. Ask what gift Christ has given you, and whether you have treated it as yours to keep or as his to share. And if you have ever felt that you have nothing to give, notice that Paul leaves no one out.

passages.t: Gifts to equip the saints and build up the body
passages.happening:
Now Paul names the gifts. Christ “gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers” (verse 11).

The reason follows: “to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ” (verse 12). And this goes on “until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ” (verse 13).

Then believers will not be like children, “tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching” (verse 14). “Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head” (verse 15). From him the whole body grows, held together by every joint, “through the work of each individual part” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The gifts in verse 11 are people. Apostles were those sent by the risen Christ to lay the church's foundation. Prophets spoke messages from God to the church. Evangelists carried the good news to new places; Philip is called one (Acts 21:8). Pastors and teachers cared for and taught the churches. The word for ‘pastor’ means a shepherd. In Greek ‘pastors and teachers’ are joined closely, and many readers think they describe one kind of leader with two sides to the work.

Now notice what these leaders are for. They do not do all the work while everyone else watches. They ‘equip the saints’, and the saints, every believer, carry out the works of ministry. The word ‘equip’ comes from a Greek verb used for mending nets and setting bones: getting something ready to do its job.

The goal is growing up. Paul pictures a ship in a storm, or a small child pushed around by every new idea. Believers who are grown up in Christ are steady. They are not moved by every clever teacher.

‘Speaking the truth in love’ holds two things together that people often pull apart. Some speak truth without love and wound people. Others speak love without truth and leave them where they are. The body grows only when both are present.

The picture at the end is of a living body. Each part has its place. When one part stops doing its work, the whole body is weaker.
passages.ot:
God had promised to give his people good shepherds: “Then I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jeremiah 3:15). And he had warned the bad ones: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). Christ's gift of pastors stands in that line, and so does the warning.

Moses once wished that every one of God's people had the Spirit: “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them” (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised that day would come (Joel 2:28). In Ephesians the Spirit is given to the whole body, and every member has work to do.
passages.hard:
Are apostles and prophets, and gifts like prophecy, still given today? Christians disagree, and the question reaches beyond this chapter. These notes do not choose.

Many in the Reformed and some other traditions hold that apostles and prophets were given for the church's first generation. Paul calls them the church's foundation (2:20), and a foundation is laid once. On this view, once the apostles had died and their teaching was written down in the New Testament, these roles, along with miraculous gifts such as prophecy, ceased. They are often called cessationists.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, and many others often called continuationists, hold that all the gifts continue until Christ returns. They point to verse 13: the gifts are given ‘until we all reach unity in the faith’, and that day has not yet come.

Between these, some see prophecy continuing in a different form, never equal to Scripture, and some see ‘apostle’ continuing in a wider sense, of missionaries who plant churches, while the apostles who saw the risen Christ were unique.

Whatever their view, Christians agree on what the chapter is for. The risen Christ gives gifts to his church so that every member is equipped to serve, and the goal is a grown-up, united body that speaks the truth in love. The site's chapter note on Ephesians 4 says the same.
passages.asks: Paul says leaders exist to equip everyone else for ministry. Ask whether you have left the work of the church to the people up front. Ask what work of ministry God has fitted you for. And ask whether you speak the truth without love, or love without the truth, and which one you need to learn.

passages.t: Put off the old self, put on the new
passages.happening:
Paul says plainly: “you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking” (verse 17). He describes that life: darkened understanding, cut off from the life of God, hearts gone hard (verse 18). “Having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity, with a craving for more” (verse 19).

“But this is not the way you came to know Christ” (verse 20). They were taught “to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires” (verse 22), “to be renewed in the spirit of your minds” (verse 23), “and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
When Paul says ‘the Gentiles’ here, he means the way of life his readers had come out of, not people of other nations as worse by birth. His readers were themselves Gentiles (2:11). He is describing the old world they once lived in, and he has already said that ‘all of us’, himself included, once lived that way (2:3).

Notice the order in verses 17 to 19. It starts in the mind: empty thinking and darkened understanding. It moves to the heart, which grows hard. Then come the actions. And it ends with ‘a craving for more’. Sin promises to satisfy, and never does. It leaves people wanting more of what did not fill them.

The picture in verses 22 to 24 is of clothes. You take off one set and put on another. Everyone understood that. Some readers think Paul has baptism in mind, since new believers may have taken off old clothes and put on new ones, though the evidence for that custom comes mostly from later than Paul.

The ‘old self’ is the person you were without Christ. The ‘new self’ is the person God is making you, ‘created to be like God’. It is God's work, a new creation. Yet Paul still tells believers to put it on. God makes it, and they wear it.
passages.ot:
God promised through Ezekiel to change people from the inside: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Paul's ‘hardness of their hearts’ and ‘renewed in the spirit of your minds’ echo that promise.

The phrase ‘created to be like God’ takes the reader back to the beginning, when God made human beings in his image (Genesis 1:27). The new self is that image being restored.
passages.asks: Paul begins with the mind, not the behaviour. Ask what you have been filling your mind with, and whether it has made your heart softer or harder. Ask what ‘craving for more’ you know well. And ask what one old habit you need to take off, and what part of the new self you need to put on in its place.

passages.t: The new life in speech, anger, work and forgiveness
passages.happening:
Now Paul shows what the new self looks like on an ordinary day.

Truth: “each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another” (verse 25).

Anger: “‘Be angry, yet do not sin.’ Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold” (verses 26-27).

Work: “He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need” (verse 28).

Words: “Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need” (verse 29).

The Spirit: “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (verse 30).

And the end of it all: “Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you” (verses 31-32).
passages.hearers:
Notice that almost every command comes with a reason. Do not lie, because we belong to one another. Do not steal, but work, so you can give. Speak words that build up, so they bring grace to the hearer. Forgive, because God forgave you. Paul does not just give rules. He shows how each one grows out of the gospel.

The word about the thief is striking. Paul does not only say ‘stop stealing’. He says work, and give. The one who used to take becomes one who shares. In that world many educated people looked down on working with your hands. Paul himself worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), and he treats honest work as a way to love others.

The sunset line fits a common ancient view that a quarrel should be settled before the day ends. The point is not a strict rule about bedtime. It is a warning about time. Anger left to sit, night after night, hardens into bitterness and gives the devil ‘a foothold’, a place to stand in your life and your friendships.

‘Do not grieve the Holy Spirit’ shows that the Spirit is not a force but a person, who can be saddened. And he grieves especially over the sins of the tongue and temper that tear a church apart.
passages.ot:
Verse 25 echoes Zechariah: “Speak truth to one another” (Zechariah 8:16).

Verse 26 quotes Psalm 4 word for word as the BSB gives it: “Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still” (Psalm 4:4). The psalm itself gives a practice for anger: lie down, look at your own heart, be still.

The thief who stops stealing keeps the old commandment, “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15), and goes further than it asks.

Israel's law joined honesty and love: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart” and “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:17-18).

And ‘grieve the Holy Spirit’ comes from Isaiah, who said of Israel in the wilderness, “But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:10).
passages.hard:
‘Be angry, yet do not sin.’ Does this mean all anger is sin? Or does it give permission for anger?

Neither. The verse gets read both ways. Some take it to mean that every angry feeling is sin. Others treat ‘Be angry’ as permission for whatever comes out. But Paul, quoting the psalm, assumes that people will be angry. He does not command anger, and he does not forbid it. He tells believers not to sin in it, and not to let it sit and harden. Five verses later he says to get rid of ‘rage and anger’, which shows he means the anger that turns into bitterness, revenge and cruel words.

Christians weigh human anger differently. Some are wary of nearly all of it and teach that it should be quieted. Others point to the prophets, and to Jesus' anger at hard hearts (Mark 3:5), and hold that anger at injustice can be right, as long as it is aimed at the wrong and not at revenge. Both agree that most everyday anger is not that kind.

This verse does not ask someone who has been wronged to pretend it did not matter, or to fix it all before sunset. Forgiveness in verse 32 lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again or staying close to a person who keeps hurting you.

If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you do with your anger at the end of the day: take it to bed, or take it to God. Ask whether your words this week have built people up or torn them down. And read verse 32 slowly. Ask whom you need to forgive, remembering how much God in Christ has forgiven you.
